en: The Secret Essence of the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, composed by Anaṅgayogin. Om! Homage to the glorious Vajrayoginī!
Having prostrated before the Lord of the World, the *Dākinījālasaṃvara*, this supreme secret and most profound mystery is written down by Anaṅgayogin. (1)
The threefold worldly accomplishment is taught by means of perishable bliss;
however, the supreme, imperishable accomplishment must be known by one who desires the reality. (2)
By those desiring the samayasattvas, [the mundane and supramundane] of the samayasattvas.
For the sake of accomplishing spiritual attainments (*siddhi*), four consecrations (*abhiṣeka*) are proclaimed as supreme:
the Vase, the Secret Consecration, that which is named the Wisdom-Knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), and furthermore, the Great Wisdom (*mahāprajñā*), which is designated as its Knowledge (*jñāna*). (3)
By the word "kumbha" (pitcher), the two breasts are meant.
From the contact with them, that which is the flowing [fluid] and the pleasure of the flow—
that is the "kalaśābhiṣeka" (vase consecration).
The bliss that arises from the entry of the secret vajra is the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*).
The bliss that arises from the radiation of the vajra into the lotus is the wisdom initiation (*prajñābhiṣeka*).

The immutable bliss that arises through passion for the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) is the fourth; furthermore, that is the "such-like" initiation (*tathābhiṣeka*), which was spoken by the Blessed One in the *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language) for the sake of accomplishing the vow (*saṃvara*).
For the sake of accomplishing supramundane attainments, the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) should be cultivated in the sequence beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Among these, three were taught by the Blessed One according to worldly convention:
loving-kindness is so called because of touching [others] with an excess of affection, as in the case of Kumbha.
The secret [brahmavihāra] arises from the entry of the vajra; compassion follows because it is superior to that;
joy arises from the state of a gladdened mind through the expansion of the vajra in the lotus;
and equanimity arises from the departure of the stains of all conceptual constructions.
And for the sake of the pure mundane conceptualization, that fourth [empowerment] is supramundane; because it is the bliss of the motionless, such is the Blessed One’s rule.
And so it has been said:
One should accomplish the supreme siddhi through the yoga of the ultimate syllable;
once the mind-vajra has been accomplished, there is nothing that is not accomplished.
The mind-vajra is twofold: the condensed mind and the luminous [mind]. The condensed mind is meditation on the action-seal (karmamudrā), while the luminous [mind] is the great seal (mahāmudrā).
And this is to be understood through the instruction of a true guru:
"Having fixed the moon of the root-lotus by means of the great yoga of Kuṇḍalinī," so it is said.
The mind attains manifoldness through the grace of the Guru’s feet. ||4||
It has been stated that there are three kinds of worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*) for the sake of accomplishing mundane siddhis.
By the Blessed One, within the single vajra-body and within a single bliss (*ānanda*), four joys (*ānanda*) have been demonstrated.
Among these, there is the joy of the body (*kāyānanda*).
Namely, through the distinction of the bliss of speech, the bliss of mind, and the bliss of gnosis.
Such drops (bindus) are also to be understood.

Here, the threefold method of perishable bliss (*kṣarasukhanaya*) is described: [the first] through the tasting of nectar (*amṛtāsvādana*), [the second] through the service of the observance (*samaya-sevā*) and so forth, and [the third] as a means for achieving worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*).
Such is the rule of the Blessed One.
For this very reason it has been said: "The fourth is the purification of gnosis, which purifies body, speech, and mind.
And so it has also been stated:
Through seeing and touching, as well as through hearing and remembering, one is liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
The *udghāṭanīyaguhyāsaṃvara* is spoken in the *sandhyābhāṣā* [esoteric language]:
"Beholding" refers to kissing and embracing;
"touching" refers to the entry of the *vajra* into the lotus.
"Hearing" is that which is the fleeting bliss produced by the striking of the vajra;
"remembering" is being deluded along with the words of the Guru;
therefore, one is liberated from everything.
For those who are sinful, it is exactly thus; there is no doubt. By not violating the *samaya*, one attains the bliss of the imperishable (*akṣarasukha*); such is the rule of the Blessed One.

And so it is said in the *Abhidhānottara*: "One should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind, devoted to the conduct of the *samaya*. The expansion of the vital winds (*prāṇāyāma*) is the image of the Buddha from the *bodhicitta*."
Regarding "the expansion":
"That again is thus; that again is thus."

The fourth state, which is free from the qualities such as vibration (*spanda*) and so forth, is that very same thing; it has been described by the Blessed One as "innate" (*sahaja*) along with the word "thus" (*tathā*).
Regarding "mundane accomplishment here":

whatever is accomplished by means of the mundane term— whether it be subterranean, terrestrial, or celestial— all that is the fruit of mundane accomplishment, categorized as inferior, middling, or superior.
Therefore, what is the use of that which has not been established, by means of which Buddhahood— the cause for the exhaustion of birth, old age, and death— does not arise for yogins?
For this very reason, the accomplishment of the body (*kāyasiddhi*) is to be cultivated by the ascetic.
The Blessed One has said: "With the mind turned inward.
This [is] the fivefold vajra-word.
In the *Śrīsamāja*, the Blessed Buddha said:
"From the vajra-paryaṅka posture, one should gaze at the mind within the jewel;
until it reaches the state of stainlessness, filled with bliss such as the motionless (*niṣpanda*) and so forth."
And so it has been said:
"Having established the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*, one should not emit the *bodhicitta*;
rather, one should meditate upon the image of the Buddha throughout the three realms without exception."
Here, by means of these two verses, the summarized meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) of this vajra-word is to be understood.
By the word *vajraparyaṅka*, the Blessed One has expressed *padma* in the intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).
"Within that jewel" refers to [the mind] being situated therein.

When the mind-vajra (cittavajra), consisting of four drops, arises within the jewel (maṇi) at the center of the vajra, then it is said that the mind has entered the interior of the jewel from the vajra-paryaṅka posture.
This is [taught] by means of the term "nispanda" and so forth, which is the intentional language (sandhābhāṣā). |||||

Embraced by Amṛtakuṇḍalī within the *aprajñā*, it consists of sixteen joys and is composed of bliss; through its retention in the *avadhūtī* from the navel up to the lotuses of the heart, throat, forehead, and crown, until purity is attained— that is the meaning of this practice.

And it is said in the *Catuṣpīṭha*: "From the mantra comes the seat of the self (*ātmapīṭha*); from the seat of the self comes the seat of the other (*parapīṭha*); from the seat of the self comes the seat of the other."
From the *parapīṭha* to the *tattvapīṭha*, until it reaches that—namely the *bodhicitta*—by means of the *saṃvara* within the *avadhūtī*; this is the sequence of the movement of the words.
Furthermore, it is stated in two verses in the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara*:
In this context, having set aside the bodhicitta contained within the jewel, that which is contained within is called the *manas*.

With that internal *manas*, which is the non-emitted bodhicitta, the yogin should meditate without exception upon that which consists of the nature of the stable and the moving, endowed with all supreme aspects, through engagement with the *karmamudrā* and engagement with the *jñānamudrā*.
That very Perfection of Wisdom, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, is emptiness;
it has been declared by the Blessed One in the *Śrīsaṃvarottara* to be the "attainment of desire," because it is a wisdom-tantra (*prajñātantra*).

Therefore it was said by the Blessed One: "One should meditate upon Mahāmudrā through the yoga of the supreme syllable. Likewise, he said: "The yogi should meditate upon the accomplishment of desire (kāmasiddhi).
Desire is great passion (mahārāga).
He alone is Vajrasattva, the supreme immutable bliss.
And thus the Blessed One spoke to Vajrapāṇi: "By the cessation of the emission of the drop, there is Buddhahood for all embodied beings."
Therefore, it is said that there is the cessation of old age and death in the world.

And so it was stated by Vajragarbha: "The ritual of worship is taught in the Root Tantra; the knower of yoga should always perform worship according to the method of wisdom and means" (*Advayasiddhi* 57, *Hevajra*).
"Yoga" (taṃ) [is defined as] the union of Caṇḍālī and Śuklā;
therefore, that [duality] ceases.
The knower of yoga should always worship that Īśvara at all times with the bliss of the imperishable through celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the application of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), O Acyuta.
"They should be served with effort so that no distinction arises.
(He)

Regarding that: (15.3) in the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the emission of semen (*śukracyavana*) is stated by the Blessed One himself in the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara* and the *Ādibuddha* to be the going to hell (*nirayagamana*) according to the distinction of the commitments (*samayabheda*). [This is so] for those who have emitted it.
From the arising of passion comes the arising of suffering;
from suffering comes the depletion of the bodily constituents for men, and from that depletion, death is said to occur.
"What is worse than this? Going to hell.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One in the *Cakrasaṃvara*: "Conventionally, sentient beings have downward-flowing semen; ultimately, they have upward-flowing semen."
"Brahmā turns back [from it], O Buddha" (He-taṃ 1.5.13).
Because he is the support of the elements (*dhātu*), because he is the destruction within his own body, and because there is no exit from the Brahma-world, the Buddha is called Vairocana;
because he is without destruction (*avināśa*),
he is called Viṣṇu.
Because the element of urine does not flow out, due to its entry into his own body and the absence of external emission, he is called Buddha Viṣṇu.
"Śiva is so called because he is eternally auspicious."
The morality (*śīla*) that is the mandala of excellence is called the Buddha Śiva because of the absence of the emission of semen;
for it is said: "All [is] established within the Self of All."
All is the source of jewels (*ratnasaṃbhava*);
that itself is the red element (*raktadhātu*), and because there is no falling away from it, there is the non-existence of suffering.
Therefore: "The end of pleasure and pain is the ultimate state; dispassion is the exhaustion of the substrates (*upadhi*)."
Abiding in the universal self, the Buddha is called "all" because his knowledge of the minds of others pervades everything through his divine eye.
This entire [teaching] is to be understood gradually by attending upon the feet of the Guru; this is the rule of the Blessed One.

Having constantly abandoned the conceit of being learned, one must understand the intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*) and so forth through the tradition of a true Guru; this is the rule of the Blessed One.

Therefore, the six-limbed meditation taught in the *Hevajra* consists of [the colors] black, red, yellow, green, blue, and white. Through the yoga of this six-limbed meditation, it is said: "The yogi [attains] up to the stage of cessation (*viramānta*), and again likewise" (*Hevajratantra* 1.8.24).
And so it has been stated: "By means of the six-limbed meditation, the state of Vajradhara is certainly accomplished."
In the *Śrī-Samājottara*, the Blessed One said:
"Withdrawal of the senses, as well as meditation, breath control, mental retention, recollection, and meditative absorption—this is held to be the six-limbed yoga. (18.140)
In this context, by the term *pratyāhāra*, the vision of the Buddha-image of the three realms [is meant],
through union with Kuṇḍalī. Here,
the Blessed One has stated that what is called *amṛtakuṇḍalī*— at the end of the intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*)— is designated as *svara*.
The summary meaning of this should be understood from the instruction of a true guru.
As for [the practice] beginning with *dhāraṇā*:
thereafter, what is called *dhyāna* is the engagement of the mind within all things that are empty.
Vitarka is the mind's grasping at an object;
vicāra is the illumination of that object.
Joy (*prīti*) is the mental application toward all phenomena.
Immovable bliss (*sukha*) is the attainment of happiness from all phenomena.
One-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is the unification of the mind with the image (*bimba*).
Thus, the five factors of dhyāna are said to be:
vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and likewise one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā); these five constitute the constituents of dhyāna.
(Gu | Sa | 18 | 143) Next, what is called *prāṇāyāma* is the obstruction of the left and right channels of the woman.
This indeed is the spring season;
it is the equal flow of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) within the central channel (*avadhūtī*). Therein, by means of the yoga of the wind, there is movement within the *avadhūtī*.
The yogi performs exhalation with the syllable Oṃ,
inhalation with the syllable Āḥ,
and retention with the syllable Huṃ, by way of the nature of the Moon, the Sun, and Rāhu.

Thus, the limb of *prāṇāyāma* is described. Following that is what is called *dhāraṇā*: the retention of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the spheres of Indra, Varuṇa, Agni, and Vāyu at the navel, the heart, and the throat.
Entry into the forehead;
there is no exit to the exterior.
The entry of the vital breath (prāṇa) into the moon is called the limb of concentration (dhāraṇā).

Then, what is called "recollection" (*anusmṛti*) is the vision of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) in the form of a reflection, free from conceptual construction; from that arises a circle of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*) whose form radiates manifold rays.
Then, [there appears] the triple world (*traidhātuka*) with its forms radiating in manifold ways.
"Battle" (raṇa) refers to what is called the limb of recollection (anusmṛti).
Following that is what is known as meditative absorption (samādhi): the attainment of imperishable bliss through devotion to the chosen deity, and the unification [of the mind] within that.
The Tathāgatas have stated that the mind, free from the duality of grasped object and grasping subject, is called a limb of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This has been taught here in brief as being within the yoga of the cultivation of the six limbs;

however, it should be understood in detail through the instruction of a true guru in the *Abhidhānaparamā* and other tantras by one who seeks the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Yoginīs.
The yogi should meditate upon the six-limbed Svādhiṣṭhāna day and night;
he swiftly attains accomplishment, as stated by Vajrabhūti himself.
(He | ta | 1 | 8 | 24) Herein lies the Blessed One’s formal proposition.
"Abandoning all thought, one should examine for a single day;
if no conviction arises therein, then these words of mine are false."
In that context, "pratyaya" refers to the cause, such as smoke and so forth;
the first is the cause characterized by smoke,
and the second has the form of a mirage.
The third has the appearance of a firefly;
the fourth is the sign of a lamp; the fifth is like a cloudless sky.
It was stated by the Blessed One in the chapter on the Māyājāla-samādhi, as follows:
"The self-arisen one born from space, the great fire of the wisdom of insight,
Vairocana of great radiance, the illuminator of the light of gnosis."
"The lamp of the world, the torch of gnosis, of great splendor, and luminous;
the fierce King of Vidyās, Lord of Mantras, the King of Mantras who accomplishes the great purpose" (Nāmasaṃgīti, 61–62).
With these two verses, the Blessed One has spoken another sign in the language of intentional terminology (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).
That which appears like a cloudless sky is "arisen from space" (*gaganodbhava*);
it is self-arisen because the mind is free from all conceptual constructions.
In this context, the fire of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) is the manifestation of gnosis.
Vairocana, the Great Radiance, is the manifestation of the moon; he is also the Illuminator of the Light of Gnosis. Jagatpradīpa, the Lamp of the World, is the manifestation of the sun.
"The torch of gnosis" is the appearance of Rāhu;
"of great brilliance and luminous" is the appearance of the sun. "The torch of gnosis" is the appearance of Rāhu.
"Of great splendor and radiant" refers to the appearance of lightning.
"The King of Vidyās, the foremost Lord of Mantras" refers to the appearance of the mind in the form of a blue-colored lunar disc.

"The King of Mantras, the accomplisher of the great purpose" is seen by the yoginīs as the appearance of the entire threefold world in all its aspects, similar to the appearances of an illusion or a dream.
By means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*).
The eight great signs are the rule of the Blessed One.
And so it is said in the *Ḍākinījāla*:

In the *Saṃvara*, the Blessed One has declared: "Success is attained for all embodied beings, as many as there are among all living creatures—gods, daityas, and humans—dwelling throughout the three realms, without exception or remainder"; and the Blessed One’s injunction is: "The yogin should cultivate the six limbs."
Furthermore, it is said in the *Vajrapañjara*:
"Therefore, one should meditate on the six-limbed [yoga], which is equal to self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*);
it is beautiful in all its limbs, delightful, and free from all attachment."
The delightful and most wonderful wheel of ḍākinīs is the self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna),
which arises in an instant through the grace of the Guru’s feet.
In the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, the second chapter on the ritual of the union with Śrī Vajrasattva,
the Blessed One has also stated:
"From one's own self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), the assembly of all Buddhas indeed arises."
The thought of awakening is eternally red, for it is the cause of the cessation of suffering;
otherwise, indeed, Buddhahood would not be attained even in tens of millions of incalculable eons.
Those who are truly realized are rare in the world; others are merely established in [external] coverings.
Indeed, those yogins who have abandoned all veils are exceedingly difficult to find.
And so it was said by the venerable Vasubandhu:
"Enlightenment is indeed the cutting off of obscurations.
There are three obscurations: the non-arising of the wholesome,..."
The incompleteness of the accumulations,
lack of mental attention, and likewise not taking the true Dharma as one's sphere of activity.
"Respect for gain, honor, and worship, and lack of compassion toward all beings.
Furthermore, it is said: "Even non-abiding nirvāṇa is an obscuration for those of the bodhisattva lineage."
Likewise, even the desire for liberation is an obscuration for Bodhisattvas; such is the detailed explanation.
Furthermore, it was stated by the Blessed One in the *Ratnacūḍa* and other Mahāyāna sūtras: "The yogi should cultivate emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects."

If there were attachment even to that emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects— by way of the thought "this alone is the essence of reality"— that too would be a cause for going to hell due to such a view.

And so it has been said: "He who possesses peaceful intelligence and understands the equality of all phenomena and sentient beings does not adhere to either phenomena or non-phenomena. Non-adherence to phenomena is their true meaning."
"And that which exceeds the goal is itself its great misfortune.
If this were so, then the undertaking of liberation would be futile.
This is the heart-essence of the Blessed One;
it is not the word of one who lacks supernormal knowledge.
The manifestation of "bondage and liberation" occurs through conventional truth; in reality, however, there is no liberation.
Thus it has been said:
"In this world, one who is bound is not liberated, nor is one who is unbound liberated."
In reality, there is no other [self] here that is either bound or liberated from bondage.
And so it has been said:
"Therefore, if intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not exist as something that undergoes alteration,
how could there be alteration?"
If existence itself does not exist at all, [how can there be non-existence?]

And in the *Svavikrāmiṇa-paripṛcchā*, it is said: "Those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who do not conceptualize— [thinking], 'There exists this thing called enlightenment, for the sake of which I am striving toward its constituent parts'— for them, the state of a Bodhisattva is far off."

Those bodhisattvas deceive the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, and there is no further elaboration on this; thus one should not have confidence in them. Both "it exists" and "it does not exist" are prohibited.
This was established by the Blessed One, the discernor of existence and non-existence;
and thus it has been said:
"Those who do not know emptiness do not know liberation."
Therefore, emptiness should indeed be understood by one who discerns both existence and non-existence.
And it has been said:
"Emptiness, characterized by the cutting off of the continuity of conceptual constructions of the auspicious and the inauspicious, has been proclaimed by the Buddha as non-dual."
"Emptiness is considered [the antidote].
And thus it has been said:
"The Victors have declared emptiness to be the relinquishing of all views."
"But those for whom emptiness itself is a view, they declared to be incurable. Thus it is said.
One who is always devoted to the Guru and always possesses a compassionate disposition, [engaged in] mantra and worship...
This will certainly be accomplished perpetually; there is no doubt.
Therefore, by means of the primordial practice itself, they attain supreme enlightenment in due time; thus, one should generate virtue by observing the lineage of the gurus. So it is said.
And so it has been said by the perfectly awakened Vajrasattva: "Emptiness has been proclaimed;
therefore, this is the teaching of Samantabhadra."
Through the yoga of space and barley, those who possess an ocean of gnosis grasp it;
then the King Vajradhara increases great bliss.
One should teach the *samaya*, which bestows the fruit of all Buddhahood,
accompanied by joyful pleasures, as well as dances, songs, instrumental music, and miraculous transformations.
The King of Vidyās is accomplished through perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
he is pleased by whatever is comfortable and by whatever actions are performed according to one's preference.
Just as even food and conduct are accomplished as the supreme syllable,
so too are the practices of eating and drinking [perfected] by means of divine ornaments and decorations.
When impelled, the supreme reality is accomplished in a single day;
one's own commitment must be constantly fulfilled, and likewise, the Tathāgatas must be constantly worshipped.
And this should always be offered to the Guru; therefore, the Guru is equal to the Buddha.
Just as the Lord Vairocana is, so too is the Guru Vajradhara.
Just as Ākāśa, O Great King, and Vajradharma, the Great Sage, and just as Samantabhadra, the Protector, so too is the Ācārya praised.
Therefore, with every effort, one should never, under any circumstances, despise the Vajrācārya, the great guru, who possesses the excellent and secret internal placement [of mantras].
Furthermore, it is said in the *Vajrapañjara*:
"One should not step over the shadow of the guru, nor his sandals, nor his wife. Those men who, out of delusion, do so carry razors."
Even when he has attained perfection himself, if a disciple does not transgress the command of his guru,
he shall suffer from leprosy in this world and dwell in hell in the next world.
By practicing deceit and hypocrisy through the display of false devotion,
one is born as one afflicted by consumption, leprosy, and other great diseases, and falls into the hells and other lower realms.
Thinking thus, a disciple who is always devoted to his guru should accomplish great success by respectfully fulfilling the guru’s command.
Thus ends the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvararahasya*.
